source_text: KATHERINA. Fie, fie! unknit that threatening unkind brow, And dart not scornful glances from those eyes To wound thy lord, thy king, thy governor: It blots thy beauty as frosts do bite the meads, Confounds thy fame as whirlwinds shake fair buds, And in no sense is meet or amiable. A woman mov’d is like a fountain troubled, Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty; And while it is so, none so dry or thirsty Will deign to sip or touch one drop of it. Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper, Thy head, thy sovereign; one that cares for thee, And for thy maintenance commits his body To painful labour both by sea and land, To watch the night in storms, the day in cold, Whilst thou liest warm at home, secure and safe; And craves no other tribute at thy hands But love, fair looks, and true obedience; Too little payment for so great a debt. Such duty as the subject owes the prince, Even such a woman oweth to her husband; And when she is froward, peevish, sullen, sour, And not obedient to his honest will, What is she but a foul contending rebel And graceless traitor to her loving lord?— I am asham’d that women are so simple To offer war where they should kneel for peace, Or seek for rule, supremacy, and sway, When they are bound to serve, love, and obey. Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth, Unapt to toil and trouble in the world, But that our soft conditions and our hearts Should well agree with our external parts? Come, come, you froward and unable worms! My mind hath been as big as one of yours, My heart as great, my reason haply more, To bandy word for word and frown for frown; But now I see our lances are but straws, Our strength as weak, our weakness past compare, That seeming to be most which we indeed least are. Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot, And place your hands below your husband’s foot: In token of which duty, if he please, My hand is ready; may it do him ease.
modern_text: KATHERINA. Fie, fie! Unknit that threatening, unkind brow, and don't dart scornful glances from those eyes to wound your lord, your king, your governor. It blots your beauty as frost bites the meadows, ruins your reputation as whirlwinds shake fair buds — and in no way is it fitting or amiable. A woman moved is like a troubled fountain: muddy, ugly, thick, stripped of beauty. And while it is so, no one — however dry or thirsty — will deign to sip or touch a drop of it. Your husband is your lord, your life, your keeper, your head, your sovereign — one who cares for you, and for your maintenance commits his body to painful labour both by sea and land, to keep watch by night in storms, by day in cold, while you lie warm at home, secure and safe. And he asks no other tribute from you but love, kind looks, and true obedience — too small a payment for so great a debt. The same duty a subject owes the prince, a woman owes her husband. And when she is contrary, peevish, sullen, sour, and not obedient to his honest will, what is she but a foul, contentious rebel, and an ungrateful traitor to her loving lord? I am ashamed that women are so simple as to offer war where they should kneel for peace, or seek rule, supremacy, and command, when they are bound to serve, love, and obey. Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth, unfit for toil and trouble in the world, except that our gentle natures and our hearts should match our outward form? Come, come, you contrary and incapable creatures! My spirit has been as big as any of yours, my heart as great, my reason perhaps more — to trade word for word and frown for frown. But now I see our lances are only straws, our strength as weak, our weakness beyond compare — seeming most what we are in truth the least. Then lower your prides, for it's no use, and place your hands beneath your husband's foot. As a token of that duty, if he please, my hand is ready — may it bring him ease.

source_text: KATHERINA. So you may lose your arms — your coat of arms. If you strike me, you're no gentleman. And if no gentleman, then no arms.
modern_text: KATHERINA. So may you lose your arms: If you strike me, you are no gentleman; And if no gentleman, why then no arms.

source_text: [_To Lucentio._] though you hit the white;
modern_text: [_To Lucentio._] though you hit the bullseye —

source_text: PETRUCHIO. Your gown? Why, yes — come, tailor, let's see it. Oh mercy, God! What masquerade stuff is here? What's this? A sleeve? It's like a demi-cannon. What — carved up and down like an apple tart? Here's snip and nip and cut and slish and slash, like a censer in a barber's shop. Why, what in the devil's name, tailor, do you call this?
modern_text: PETRUCHIO. Thy gown? Why, ay: come, tailor, let us see’t. O mercy, God! what masquing stuff is here? What’s this? A sleeve? ’Tis like a demi-cannon. What, up and down, carv’d like an apple tart? Here’s snip and nip and cut and slish and slash, Like to a censer in a barber’s shop. Why, what i’ devil’s name, tailor, call’st thou this?
